books.section: Topic 4.7 Expanding Democracy, A. Participatory Democracy and an Expanding Electorate

stimulus.text: Paraphrase of Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 6, Topic 4.7 A: In the 1820s, most states reduced or removed property qualifications for voting, so most free white males could vote. The push was strongest in the newly admitted states of the West. Ohio, admitted in 1803, led the way, letting any voter hold public office. Between 1816 and 1821, six new states also wrote broader voting rules into their constitutions. Land was cheaper and more widely available in the West, so fewer men there were landless. In the 1820s, older states felt pressure from popular movements to follow, and most reduced property qualifications, though many still required voters to be taxpayers. Historians estimate that about 90 percent of adult white men could vote by 1840.
stimulus.source_note: Secondary text: paraphrase of Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 6, Topic 4.7 A. Paraphrased, not quoted.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: The passage best supports which conclusion about voting in the United States by 1840?

options.text: Every adult in the United States could vote
options.misconception: The passage counts only free white males, and about 90 percent of them, not every adult.

options.text: Women had won the vote in most states
options.misconception: The passage is about free white males; it says nothing about women voting.

options.text: About nine in ten adult white men were eligible to vote
Property qualifications still barred most white men from voting in 1840
options.misconception: Most states had reduced or removed the property rules by then.

rationales.A: The 90 percent figure covers adult white men only, not every adult.
rationales.B: The passage says nothing about women voting; its subject is free white males.
rationales.C: Historians estimate that about 90 percent of adult white men could vote by 1840, after most states cut or dropped property rules.
rationales.D: Most states had reduced or removed the property rules, so most white men could vote.
rationales.general:
1. Read the number. Historians put eligibility at about 90 percent of adult white men by 1840.
2. Check who counts. The passage speaks of free white males only, so the figure leaves out women, enslaved people, and free Black men.
3. Ask what changed. Most states reduced or removed property qualifications in the 1820s, which is what pushed the share so high.
Background: Many states still required voters to be taxpayers, so even the 90 percent figure had a floor under it.
Remember: a big number can still describe a narrow group, so always ask who is counted.
